problem:
Let $f(x,y,z)$ be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where $a=⟨3,2,5⟩$ and $b=⟨1,4,1⟩$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively. If $f(a)=2$ and $f(b)=3,$ then what is missing from the statement below?

*The mean value theorem states that there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that $\text{_______________}\,.$ *

feedback.problem: Let $f(x,y)$ be a function that is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where $a=⟨-3,5⟩$ and $b=⟨2,1⟩$ are the position vectors of $A$ and $B,$ respectively. If $f(a)=-2$ and $f(b)=4,$ then according to the mean value theorem, which of the following must be true for some point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

In our case, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(b)-f(a) & =∇f(c)·(b-a) \\ 4-(-2) & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot (⟨2,1⟩-⟨-3,5⟩) \\ 6 & =⟨{f}_{x}(c),{f}_{y}(c)⟩\cdot ⟨5,-4⟩ \\ 6 & =5{f}_{x}(c)-4{f}_{y}(c).\end{aligned}
$$
